title: Vinogradov’s least quadratic nonresidue conjecture
formal:
For an odd prime \(p\), let \(n(p)\) be the least positive quadratic nonresidue modulo \(p\), defined below. Is it true, unconditionally, that
\[\forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists P_\varepsilon\in\mathbb N\ \forall p\ge P_\varepsilon\text{ odd prime},\qquad n(p)\le p^{\varepsilon}?\]
Equivalently, is \(n(p)=p^{o(1)}\) as \(p\) tends to infinity through the odd primes? The threshold may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on the prime. No unproved analytic hypothesis is assumed.
why: A small quadratic nonresidue is a basic witness used in finite-field arithmetic, and its size measures how long the initial integers can all behave like squares modulo a prime. The conjecture asks for uniform cancellation strong enough to beat every fixed power of the modulus. It would cross a long-standing barrier in character sums and bound the range of deterministic searches for such witnesses; subpolynomial size in the modulus is not the same claim as polynomial size in its bit length.

sentences: A quadratic nonresidue is a nonzero residue that is not a square modulo the prime.
Vinogradov’s conjecture says that the least positive one eventually lies below every fixed positive power of the prime.
The threshold may depend on the exponent, but the bound must cover every sufficiently large odd prime.
Conditional logarithmic-square estimates and almost-all-prime results do not establish this unconditional statement.
A refutation would require one fixed positive exponent and arbitrarily large primes violating its bound.

definitions:
For integers \(a,b\) and a positive integer \(p\), the congruence \(a\equiv b\pmod p\) means that \(p\) divides \(a-b\). An integer \(a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\) if there exists \(x\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\) with \(x^2\equiv a\pmod p\); otherwise it is a quadratic nonresidue. Define
\[n(p)=\min\{a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}:\forall x\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\},\ x^2\not\equiv a\pmod p\}.\]
For an odd prime, exactly half of its nonzero residue classes are squares, so the set is nonempty. Representatives are ordered as ordinary positive integers; this is not the least absolute value among positive and negative representatives. Multiples of \(p\) are not counted as nonresidues.

The domain is all odd primes, not composite moduli, almost all primes, or one prescribed congruence class. The prime \(2\) is omitted because every nonzero residue modulo \(2\) is a square. Real powers have the convention \(p^\varepsilon=\exp(\varepsilon\log p)\), where \(\log\) is the natural logarithm.

The statement can equivalently be expressed using only integer powers:
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists P_k\in\mathbb N\ \forall p\ge P_k\text{ odd prime},\qquad n(p)^k\le p.\]
Likewise, the subpolynomial notation means \(\lim_{p\to\infty,\ p\ \mathrm{prime}}\log n(p)/\log p=0\). The source writes \(n(p)=O_\varepsilon(p^\varepsilon)\); since its claim quantifies over every positive exponent, the implicit constant can be absorbed by using a smaller exponent and increasing the threshold. The unit-leading-constant formulation above is therefore equivalent. The conjecture asks for existence of the thresholds, without an extra requirement to compute them effectively.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal statement, or a Lean-checked refutation. A refutation must establish a fixed \(\varepsilon_0>0\) and arbitrarily large odd primes \(p\) with \(n(p)>p^{\varepsilon_0}\). A finite numerical exception cannot refute an eventual bound. A result for almost all primes, a bound with one fixed positive exponent, or a theorem assuming GRH or Elliott–Halberstam is insufficient without also proving the necessary hypothesis.

context_blocks.text: Tao states the conjecture with a constant depending on the chosen exponent and records the general unconditional Burgess bound \(n(p)=O_\eta(p^{1/(4\sqrt e)+\eta})\) for every \(\eta>0\), where \(e=\exp(1)\). That fixed positive base exponent does not imply the conjecture.

The introduction records Ankeny’s stronger \(O((\log p)^2)\) bound under the generalized Riemann hypothesis. It also notes results for almost all primes. Both are separated from the unconditional all-primes target.

Tao’s Theorem 1.3 proves that the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture on primes in arithmetic progressions implies Vinogradov’s conjecture. This is a conditional implication, not an unconditional resolution.

Quesada-Herrera’s June 2025 slides continue to display the Burgess exponent as the unconditional bound. The following slide discusses a better constant in a logarithmic-square estimate and explicitly assumes GRH. That improvement therefore does not settle the statement here.
